references.text: The command to eat the Passover meal with a belt fastened around the waist: "This is how you are to eat it: With your cloak tucked into your belt, your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand" (Exodus 12:11). Luke 12:35 uses the same image of having one's loins girded as an expression of readiness.

Proverbs speaks of a lamp that is not extinguished: "She sees that her trading is profitable, and her lamp does not go out at night" (Proverbs 31:18). The image of the burning lamp expresses vigilance and diligence, just as the burning lamps in Luke 12:35 symbolize readiness.
The parable of the ten virgins in Matthew 25:1-13 is about having one's lamps lit and being ready for the bridegroom's arrival, a parallel image to the burning lamps in Luke 12:35.

Paul uses the same image of standing with the belt of truth fastened around the waist: "Stand firm then! With the belt of truth buckled around your waist" (Ephesians 6:14). The image of girded loins expresses spiritual readiness, as in Luke 12:35.

Peter uses the same expression: "Therefore, with minds that are alert and fully sober, set your hope on the grace to be brought to you when Jesus Christ is revealed" (1 Peter 1:13). The call to gird up one's loins is a picture of mental and spiritual readiness, directly parallel to Jesus' words in Luke 12:35.

The context in Luke 12:40 explains the reason for this readiness: "Be ready too, because the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect him." This provides the theological basis for the exhortation in verse 35.
Jesus' exhortation to keep watch in Matthew 24:42-44, because one does not know when the Lord is coming, is a parallel to the call for readiness in Luke 12:35.
Paul's exhortation to wake up from sleep and put on the armor of light (Romans 13:11-14) has a close thematic connection to the image of burning lamps and readiness in Luke 12:35.
